draft.title: Domestic violence and the law
card: An apprehended violence order (AVO) is a court order that protects a person from violence, threats, harassment or stalking. In NSW, an apprehended domestic violence order (ADVO) is the kind used when the people are in a domestic relationship.

An AVO sets conditions for the person it is made against, such as not approaching or contacting the protected person. A court or a police officer can apply for one, and the protected person can also apply.
Breaching an AVO is a criminal offence. The order itself is not a criminal charge, but ignoring its conditions can lead to one.

Coercive control is a pattern of behaviour used to control or dominate a partner, such as isolating them or monitoring them. From 2024, NSW made coercive control in a current or former intimate relationship a crime.
draft.remember: An AVO protects a person by setting conditions, and coercive control is now a crime in NSW.

a.q: Why is coercive control treated as a crime in NSW intimate relationships?
opts: It is a pattern of controlling behaviour, not one act
It only applies to couples who are married to each other
It replaces the need for apprehended violence orders
It is limited to physical harm caused by a partner
a.why: Coercive control is a pattern of behaviour used to dominate a partner, so the law reaches harm beyond a single act. It covers current or former intimate relationships, not only marriages, and it does not replace AVOs.
a.clue: Think about what the behaviour looks like over time.

b.q: Dev has an ADVO against him that bars him from contacting his former partner Mia. He sends her several messages. What is the legal position?
opts: He has breached the order, which is a criminal offence
He has committed no offence, as an ADVO is only civil
He has breached the order, but only a civil penalty applies
He has committed no offence unless Mia is physically hurt
b.why: Breaching the conditions of an AVO is a criminal offence, so contacting Mia can lead to a charge. The tempting idea that an order is only civil is wrong, because the order itself is not a charge but breaking it is a crime.
b.clue: What happens when the conditions of the order are ignored?

a.best: It is a pattern of controlling behaviour, not one act

b.best: He has breached the order, which is a criminal offence

problems.detail: "A court or a police officer can apply for one" is wrong. A court does not apply for an AVO; it makes the order. Police apply, and the protected person (or someone on their behalf) can apply. It should say police or the protected person can apply, and a court makes the order.

The question asks "Why" coercive control is treated as a crime, but the right option only describes what coercive control is (a pattern, not one act). The card never explains why it was criminalised, so the question and answer do not match. Rewording to "What best describes coercive control under NSW law?" would fix it.
